SBAC Student Growth Norms:
Theoretical Considerations and Results

 Damian Betebenner
 Center for Assessment

 Minneapolis, Minnesota
 May 15th, 2019

Background
 • Beginning in Spring 2018, the Center for
 Assessment began working with SBAC to create
 growth norms and SGPs using SBAC consortium
 data.
 • Project was led by Drs. Damian Betebenner and
 Joseph Martineau from the Center for Assessment.
 • Project was conducted between June, 2018 and
 February, 2019.

5/15/19

Background
 • Project goals
 – Provide a brief overview of student growth and the
 models used nationally.
 – Analyze SBAC data using 3 student growth models:
 • Gain scores
 • Gain score norms.
 • Norms conditioning on prior score(s) (Student Growth
 Percentiles)
 – Present summary results for the different models using
 SBAC data
 – Provide recommendations on how growth norms could
 best be used.

5/15/19

SBAC Data
 • Three years of longitudinal SBAC data was
 provided: 2014-2015, 2015-2016, and 2016-2017.
 • Data comprised student results from 10 SBAC
 member states.
 • No personally identifiable information was
 provided as part of the data.
 • Limited student demographic information was
 provided as part of the data.
 • No school or district identifiers were provided in
 the data.

Growth Analyses
 • Three classes of growth analyses were conducted
 with the SBAC data:
 – Gain score analyses using the SBAC vertical scale
 – Gain score norm analyses
 – Norms conditioning on prior score(s) (Student Growth
 Percentiles)
 • Using current year score for dependent variable and single
 prior (with and without measurement error correction)
 • Using gain score for dependent variable and single prior (with
 and without measurement error correction)

5/15/19

Growth Analyses
 • All analyses were successfully conducted using the
 R software environment.
 • No substantial issues with ceiling/floor (HOSS/
 LOSS) were observed.
 – However, there appear to be different LOSS/HOSS
 rules being applied in different states.
 – At the extremes of the scales where LOSS/HOSS rules
 differ, growth results would not be comparable across
 states with different ceilings/floors.

5/15/19

Gain Score Analyses
 • The most intuitive and straightforward growth
 analysis method is gain/difference scores.
 • The SBAC vertical scale permits scores from
 adjacent grades in the same content area to be
 subtracted to provide a gain/loss for each student
 with two such scores.
 • Because each score is an unbiased estimate of the
 student’s true score, the gain score is an unbiased
 estimate of the student’s true gain score.

5/15/19

Gain Score Analyses
 • Despite their intuitive nature, gain scores are
 difficult to interpret because their magnitude
 depends upon:
 – Content area
 – Grade
 – Year
 – Prior score
 • In addition, because of these dependencies
 aggregation (and comparison) of gains is
 problematic.

5/15/19

Gain Score Norm Analyses
 • One way of eliminating the gain score dependency on
 content area, grade, and year is to create gain norms
 (percentile ranks for gains).
 • Gain score norms maintain a dependency upon prior scores.

5/15/19

Student Growth Percentiles
 • To eliminate dependency upon prior scores one can
 condition upon prior score(s).
 • Student growth percentiles (SGPs) are growth
 norms conditioned upon prior score(s).
 • There are several ways of calculating SGPs:
 – With or without measurement error correction.
 – Using the final score or the gain score for the
 dependent variable in the regression analyses.

5/15/19

Student Growth Percentiles
 • Properties of SGPs
 – Uniformly distributed
 – Uncorrelated with prior achievement
 – Uncorrelated from year-to-year. That is, no relationship
 between a student’s SGP from one year to the next.
 – Central tendency of SGPs is 50. That is, mean/median
 SGPs for groups tend toward 50.
 – Growth norms don’t address questions of ”good
 enough” or ”adequate” growth. See criterion-referenced
 growth.

5/15/19

Student Growth Percentiles
 • There are several types of norm-groups that can be
 used to create the growth norms:
 – Consortium level norms using all students in the
 consortium.
 – State level norms that create a different growth norms
 for each state.
 – Weighted consortium level norms where states are
 proportionally weighted to adjust for state size.
 • Analyses for this report used consortium norms.

5/15/19

5/15/19

Recommendations
 • The SBAC vertical scale provides the foundation
 for monitoring student year-to-year growth.
 • Technical and non-technical stakeholders will
 calculate gain scores.
 • Supplementing gain-scores with growth norm
 information will help stakeholders interpret the
 gain.
 • There are many ways in which growth norm
 information can be communicated besides a
 percentile rank.
